title: An extremely unofficial first look at the 2028 Senate map
contentHtml:
I wasn’t planning to publish anything today, but I had some time on my train down to Washington, where we’ll be doing a live episode of Still Counting tomorrow morning at Crooked Con. Since it’s a mostly progressive audience, we figure we’ll spend most of our time talking about how Democrats might respond in the wake of their extraordinary night. And then we’ll tackle the equally challenging question of how Republicans might try to clean up after their disaster, probably on our regular Wednesday show. Although I have to say that Trump’s decision to replace Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller as his chief of staff isn’t exactly rational behavior given the scope of the Republican defeat.

While doing the prep for these shows, though, I found I needed a clearer mental picture of the Senate landscape in 2028. Democrats are probably going to end up with 56 Senate seats this year: prediction markets have Scott Colom and Mary Peltola as 98 percent favorites to eventually be declared the winners in Mississippi (!!!!!) and Alaska, respectively. That’s a lot of Democrats. Other than Sherrod Brown, whose victory came in a special election so he’ll be on the ballot again in 2028, the Democrats elected this year won’t face voters again until 2032. They’ll serve for the entirety of the 48th President’s first term.

But having a lot of Democrats comes with a lot of responsibility for the party. So I wanted to get some sense of how large the Democratic majority might (or might not) be in 2029 when the next president is sworn in given three scenarios:

  • Tsunami 2.0. A repeat of Tuesday night, with another D +13 environment on the national House ballot.

  • A good-but-not-great Democratic night. A +5 national environment. Think roughly a climate like 2012, except Democrats realize the environment more efficiently in the House than they did in that election.1

  • A modest Republican win. An R +3 House popular vote, roughly like in 2024.

On the train, I found myself jotting down a series of provisional race ratings using the categories that groups like Cook Political Report typically use, from “Solid R” to toss-up to “Solid D”.

Yes, I’m going to share those ratings. No, you shouldn’t take them all that seriously. Yes, I’m going to put them behind the paywall because it makes it less likely that they’ll be taken out of context. I do not want to overbill or overpromise what these reflect:

  • They are not FLIPR ratings.

  • There is not extensive race-by-race commentary, just a few bullet points. I am reserving the right to do a deeper dive on 2028 Senate races early in the new year, and we probably will do that.

But I felt like I needed to give myself at least some rough, thin-sliced answers to the two questions posed by the subheadline. If Democrats finish with 56 seats this year, do Republicans even have a path back toward re-flipping the Senate in 2028? And if a Democrat wins the presidency, how large might his or her majorities be?

FLIPR sees another blue year in 2028 if Trump remains this unpopular

But isn’t it a little generous to Democrats to give them two winning scenarios while Republicans get only one relatively modest win? Actually, I’m not so sure, because there was one last piece of work I asked of FLIPR 🐬 before he begins his much-deserved trip to the Bahamas.
